name: Soviet Union
line: Live the shared task, the kitchen table and the long reading.

quote.text: The Earth is the cradle of humanity, but one cannot live in the cradle forever.

quotes.source: The Master and Margarita, written 1928 to 1940

quotes.text: The line dividing good and evil cuts through the heart of every human being. And who is willing to destroy a piece of his own heart?
quotes.source: The Gulag Archipelago, vol. 1, part 1, ch. 4, trans. Thomas P. Whitney

quotes.text: I was with my people then, there, where my people, unfortunately, were.

quotes.source: Said at launch, 12 April 1961; usually rendered "Off we go" or "Let’s go"

quotes.text: Poetry is respected only in this country: people are killed for it.
quotes.source: As recalled by Nadezhda Mandelstam in Hope Against Hope

words.meaning: Comrade; companion
words.usage: Before 1917 it meant a companion or colleague. The Soviet state made it the form of address between citizens.

words.meaning: A work team or group that shares a task
words.usage: The workplace, the class and the street team were all kollektivy, each with its own pressures and loyalties.

words.meaning: A country house or garden plot
words.usage: Allotments of about six hundred square metres let millions of city families grow vegetables and spend summers outside.

words.meaning: Unpaid voluntary work on a Saturday
words.usage: It began in 1919 as a call to work for free on a Saturday. Later it was often expected rather than chosen.

words.meaning: Morning exercise; literally "charging"
words.usage: A short routine of stretching and movement to charge the body for the day.

words.meaning: A communal apartment shared by several families
words.usage: After 1917 large flats were divided among families who shared one kitchen and one bathroom.

words.meaning: Self-published; banned writing copied by hand or typewriter
words.usage: Readers passed typed copies from hand to hand and often had to return them within a night.

words.meaning: Kitchen
words.usage: In late Soviet flats the kitchen was the room for talk, tea and frankness.

words.meaning: The educated class of writers, teachers, scientists and thinkers
words.usage: A word with a heavy history: a social duty as much as a social group.

words.meaning: Soul; inner life; warmth
words.usage: Used for the whole inner person. To speak "po dusham" is to talk heart to heart.

words.meaning: A deep, restless sadness without a clear cause
words.usage: Nabokov wrote that no single English word renders all its shades.

words.meaning: Tea
words.usage: Served strong from a pot, diluted with hot water, often with jam or a sugar cube.

words.meaning: A metal urn that keeps water hot for tea
words.usage: Literally "self-boiler". The centre of a table where people stay a long time.

words.meaning: Informal connections used to get things done
words.usage: A favour for a favour. In a shortage economy, who you knew mattered as much as what you earned.

words.meaning: Shortage; goods that were hard to obtain
words.usage: Anything scarce, from books to boots, was "defitsit" and prized.

words.meaning: Queue
words.usage: Waiting in line was part of daily life, and a place to trade news.

words.meaning: A member of the Young Pioneers, the children’s organisation
words.usage: Founded in 1922. Summer camps, red neckerchiefs and collective activities.

words.meaning: An exceptionally productive worker; a record-breaker
words.usage: Named for the miner Aleksei Stakhanov, whose 1935 record was heavily staged for publicity.

words.meaning: Five-year plan
words.usage: The state’s way of setting production targets. The first began in 1928.

words.meaning: Fellow traveller; also the first artificial satellite
words.usage: The word means "one who travels with" and passed into English in 1957.

words.meaning: Cosmonaut; a space traveller
words.usage: Soviet spacefarers were a national romance of the 1960s.

words.meaning: Restructuring
words.usage: The reform programme announced by Mikhail Gorbachev from 1985.

words.meaning: Openness; speaking out
words.usage: Policy of public candour from the mid 1980s that allowed long-banned books and histories into print.

words.meaning: The Thaw
words.usage: The relaxation after Stalin’s death. Named after a 1954 novel by Ilya Ehrenburg.

words.meaning: Stagnation
words.usage: The name later given to the Brezhnev years, a period of calm and decay.

words.meaning: People of the sixties; the generation of the Thaw
words.usage: Poets, filmmakers and scientists who believed reform from within was possible.

words.meaning: Grandmother; an older woman
words.usage: The keeper of family food and memory.

words.meaning: Perhaps; hoping it works out
words.usage: A habit of trusting luck. A shrug that is half fatalism, half resourcefulness.

words.meaning: Homeland
words.usage: Rooted in the word for birth and kin. Heavy with feeling and often with state use.

words.meaning: Peace; world; also the old village commune
words.usage: Before the spelling reform of 1918, peace and world were written differently. The reform merged them into one short word.

words.meaning: A mildly fermented drink made from rye bread
words.usage: Sold in summer from yellow tanks on city streets.

words.meaning: Let’s go; off we go
words.usage: Gagarin’s word at the launch of Vostok 1 on 12 April 1961.

practices.name: Zaryadka
practices.instructions: Stand by an open window or outside. Spend ten minutes on a plain routine of stretching, bending and moving every joint, with no equipment: neck circles, arm swings, side bends, squats, a short jog on the spot. Breathe through the nose. End by standing still for a count of ten and noticing how the body feels. Do it at the same time each day.
practices.why: For generations, morning exercise was a shared daily habit broadcast on radio and later television. The idea is modest and sturdy: the day begins by calling the body to order.
variations: Do it to a recording of a march or a waltz.
Do it with a neighbour or family member.
Take a ten-minute walk instead, no phone.

practices.name: Strong tea and black bread
practices.instructions: Brew a glass of strong tea and have it with a slice of dark rye bread and a spoonful of jam, or a pinch of salt on the bread. Sit down to it. Eat and drink slowly, and look out of the window. In Russian homes tea is the beginning of any conversation, and the first kettle of the day is a small ceremony.
practices.why: Chai from a samovar or a pot, strong, with jam or sugar, is what makes a long conversation possible. Black rye bread with a little salt is the most ordinary food in the culture and the most prized.
variations: Add a slice of lemon.
Make a second glass for someone else.
Drink it from a glass in a metal holder if you have one.

practices.name: Read the news twice
practices.instructions: Pick one story and read it in two different sources, then ask: what does each one say, and what does each leave out? Write one sentence on the difference. The Soviet reader learned to read between the lines. It is a good habit for any reader of any news in any country.
practices.why: Soviet readers learned to read between the lines of official papers, and passed banned writing by hand as samizdat. The skill of reading what is not said is still useful.
variations: Read an old newspaper and see what has aged.
Read the same story in two languages.
Ask what the story wants you to feel.

practices.name: Sit before you go
practices.instructions: Before you leave the house, sit for one minute in silence with your coat on, and think of where you are going and what you need. It is an old Russian custom: sit a moment before a journey, so nothing is forgotten, and so you set out with a calm head. Then stand and go.
practices.why: The custom of sitting before a journey is still kept in Russian families. It is both practical, to remember keys and papers, and ceremonial, to take a moment before the road.
variations: Do it before every outing today.
Do it with someone else and say nothing.
Do it before a hard meeting.

practices.name: A plain kasha breakfast
practices.instructions: Cook a small pan of kasha, buckwheat porridge, in water with a pinch of salt for fifteen minutes, then stir in a knob of butter. Eat it hot with a glass of kefir or milk. It is a plain staple that fed millions. Notice how well a simple warm bowl carries you through the morning.
practices.why: Kasha has been the everyday porridge of Russia and the Soviet Union for centuries. It is cheap, filling, and quietly delicious with butter.
variations: Add a fried egg.
Make it with milk and a spoon of jam.
Make enough to share.

practices.name: Learn four lines by heart
practices.instructions: Choose four lines of poetry and learn them by heart this morning: Pushkin, Akhmatova, Tsvetaeva, Mayakovsky, or a poem you love in any language. Say it aloud three times, then once without the page. Carry it with you. Russians have long memorised poems, and many people could recite them whole.
practices.why: Memorising poetry was an everyday habit in Russia and the Soviet Union, and in the camps people kept poems alive by heart. A poem you know by heart cannot be taken from you.
variations: Learn it with a friend and say it to each other.
Learn one stanza a day for a week.
Say it while walking.

practices.name: The common task
practices.instructions: Choose one shared place: a stairwell, a courtyard, a classroom, a park bench, a shared kitchen. Spend thirty unpaid minutes making it better with your hands: sweep, wipe, sort, repair, plant. Do it where others will use it, and do not announce it. Notice what it is to work for something no one owns alone.
practices.why: The subbotnik began in 1919 as a voluntary Saturday of unpaid work and was later made routine. The better half of the idea survives the politics: shared places need shared care.
variations: Do it with a friend or a neighbour.
Do it for a place that belongs to no one in particular, such as a street corner.
Spend the thirty minutes on a repair you have put off.

practices.name: A game of chess
practices.instructions: Play a game of chess with someone, in person or online, and think of the schools and factories where it was taught. Play slowly. When it is done, shake hands and talk about one moment that turned the game. If you have no partner, solve a chess puzzle or replay a famous game. The state taught it to millions.
practices.why: Chess was taught in Soviet schools, factories and Pioneer palaces, and the country produced many of the world’s champions. It was a game for everyone.
variations: Play with a child.
Play a speed game and a slow one.
Study one opening.

practices.name: Quiet hunting
practices.instructions: Go out and look for something patiently in nature: mushrooms, berries, feathers, a bird you have not seen. Russians call mushroom picking quiet hunting, tikhaya okhota. Take a basket or a bag, a knife if you know what you are doing, and a friend. Only pick what you can identify for certain, or only look.
practices.why: Mushroom picking is a national passion in Russia and across the former Soviet lands. It teaches patience, and the sense that the forest is a larder as well as a place.
variations: Hunt for leaves or stones instead.
Look for one bird for half an hour.
Go with an older person who knows the forest.

practices.name: Say it plainly
practices.instructions: Choose one thing you need to say today and say it in plain words, with no hints and no padding. Write it first in one sentence, then say it aloud. A person who says what they mean is a rarity and a gift. Notice what happens when you do. Where it is hard, be kind in the sentence, but not vague.
practices.why: This Onda’s rule is to say plainly what you mean. In a country of official language, plain speech among friends was valued above all, and the kitchen was where it lived.
variations: Say it in a text, then a call.
Ask someone else to say it plainly to you.
Cross out half the words and keep the rest.

practices.name: Talk in the queue
practices.instructions: The next time you wait in a line, a bus stop, a shop, a waiting room, talk to someone near you. Ask a question: have you been waiting long? What are you hoping to find? The Soviet queue was a social place where news and advice passed. Make yours one for ten minutes.
practices.why: Queues, ocheredi, were a daily fact of Soviet life, and people turned them into a social space. You do not have to enjoy waiting to enjoy the people waiting with you.
variations: Offer to hold a place.
Ask the person ahead for a tip.
Bring two cups of tea.

practices.name: An hour at the dacha
practices.instructions: Spend half an hour tending something green: a garden bed, a window box, a few pots. Pull weeds, water, tie up, pick. Millions of Soviet families grew potatoes, cucumbers and berries at a small country plot called a dacha. If you have no plot, tend a houseplant very thoroughly.
practices.why: The dacha is a small country house with a garden, a beloved Russian institution. Many families grew a large part of their food there and spent every weekend working and resting there.
variations: Plant something and share the first harvest.
Help a neighbour with their plot.
Eat something you grew or picked.

practices.name: Kitchen table
practices.instructions: Pick one person and one pot of tea. Sit at a table with phones out of sight. Talk for at least forty minutes about something that matters to you both: a book, a worry, a plan, a memory. Ask the second question before offering your own view. Do not solve the world. If you live alone, write a long letter by hand and send it the next day.
practices.why: In the late Soviet decades the kitchen was where people spoke freely, away from official language. It shows what conversation can be when time and trust are given.
variations: Invite someone you have not spoken with at length in a year.
Add one question you have never asked this person.
Keep a short list of what you learned.

practices.name: The long reading
practices.instructions: Read one book from the Soviet or Russian tradition, a few pages at a time, for thirty minutes with no screen nearby. Read slowly, with a pencil. Stop on one sentence and copy it by hand into a notebook. If the book is long, treat it like a companion rather than a task. Resist the urge to summarise it aloud on the same day.
practices.why: Reading was central to Soviet life, partly because some writing could only be read in secret. Read slowly, a book becomes more than information. It becomes company.
variations: Read aloud to someone for ten of the thirty minutes.
Copy one page of a poem by hand.
Return to the same chapter three evenings in a row.

practices.name: Letter by hand
practices.instructions: Write a real letter on paper to one person you care about. Tell them something specific about your week, ask them a question, and sign it by hand. Post it, or hand it over. No screens while you write.
practices.why: Letters were the thread that held families and friendships together across the Soviet Union. A letter is slow, personal and private, which is exactly why it still works.
variations: Write to someone you have not spoken to in a year.
Write a postcard instead.
Write one to your future self.

practices.name: Write it down before the day ends
practices.instructions: Before you sleep, write a short entry in a notebook: what happened, what you saw, one thing someone said, one thing you want to remember. Be specific. Remember who helped you today, and say so on the page. A kept record is how a day becomes yours. Soviet diaries are now a major source for historians.
practices.why: Keeping a record is one of this Onda’s rules. Diaries and letters of ordinary people are how the Soviet century is known, beyond the official line.
variations: Write with a pencil.
Write a line for each person you spoke to.
Write only what no one else would know.

practices.name: Sing with a guitar or without
practices.instructions: Sing a song you love, one of the bard songs of Bulat Okudzhava, a folk song, a lullaby, a hymn, a rock song, or just hum. Sing it to a friend, or to the kitchen. If you play guitar, play it. If you do not, clap. The bard tradition was one voice and six strings, in kitchens and on camping trips, about ordinary feelings.
practices.why: The bard song tradition of the Soviet Union, led by Okudzhava, Vysotsky and others, spread by hand-copied tape. It was music for people and not for stadiums.
variations: Sing with a recording and then without.
Teach someone a verse.
Write four lines of your own and sing them.

practices.name: A hot bath, the banya way
practices.instructions: Make a long, hot, restful bath or shower the centre of your evening, ideally with friends, tea and a little dry sauna if you have one. The banya is a weekly ritual of heat, birch twigs and tea. If you are not well or have a heart condition, keep it warm, not hot. Come out clean, loose and sleepy.
practices.why: The banya, the steam bath, is the great communal ritual of Russian life, a place for cleaning, health and conversation. A hot bath is a modest cousin you can have anywhere.
variations: Add a cup of tea after.
Go to a sauna with a friend.
Do it as the last thing before bed.

practices.name: A day out of town
practices.instructions: Take a free day and go out of town, to a forest, a lake, a village, or a friend’s garden. Take a basket, a flask of tea and something to eat. Walk, pick, sit, talk. Millions of Soviet families escaped to the dacha on weekends, and the rhythm of country days is the same anywhere. Come back tired and clean.
practices.why: The weekend trip to the dacha or the forest was the great Soviet escape: berries, mushrooms, bonfires, tea on the porch. It is a day of enough and not too much.
variations: Go by train or bus.
Go with the whole family.
Cook something over a fire.

practices.name: Spot the space station
practices.instructions: Look up when the International Space Station is due to pass, using a free tracking site, and watch it move across the sky like a bright star. Think of Gagarin, Tereshkova and Korolev, and of everyone who has lived in orbit. Say poyekhali, off we go, the word Gagarin said at launch. Then go to bed a little taller.
practices.why: The Soviet space programme sent the first satellite in 1957 and the first person into orbit in 1961. The station overhead carries that story on, and anyone can watch it pass.
variations: Go with a child and tell them about Gagarin.
Watch a Soviet film about space first.
Spot it three nights in a row.

immersePlan.name: Read a chapter of The Master and Margarita
immersePlan.text: Open Bulgakov’s novel about a devil who visits Moscow in the 1930s, a satire, a love story and a retelling of Pilate. Read the first chapter, and note how a cat, a conjuror and a poet appear. Enjoy the mischief.

immersePlan.name: Read the start of Roadside Picnic
immersePlan.text: Read the opening of the Strugatskys’ science fiction novel about a zone left by visitors. It is the source of Tarkovsky’s Stalker. Notice how matter-of-fact the strange is made.

immersePlan.name: Read Akhmatova’s Requiem
immersePlan.text: Read Anna Akhmatova’s cycle of poems about waiting outside a prison for news of her son. It is short and hard, and one of the great poems of the century. Read it slowly, aloud if you can.

immersePlan.name: Watch The Cranes Are Flying
immersePlan.text: Watch the wartime love story, the only Soviet film to win the Palme d’Or at Cannes. Notice the camera, which moves like a bird, and the faces.

immersePlan.name: Watch Moscow Does Not Believe in Tears
immersePlan.text: Watch the story of three women in Moscow across twenty years. It won the Academy Award for best foreign film. Notice the details of flats, lifts, canteens and dreams.

immersePlan.name: Watch part of Man with a Movie Camera
immersePlan.text: Watch twenty minutes of Vertov’s day of city life, with no actors or titles. Watch the cutting, the trams, the faces. It is a landmark of editing and a pleasure to watch.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Peter and the Wolf
immersePlan.text: Play Prokofiev’s tale for children, written for a Moscow theatre in 1936. Each character is an instrument. Listen once and guess who is who before you read the key.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Bulat Okudzhava
immersePlan.text: Play a few songs by the poet with a guitar and a quiet voice, who shaped the bard tradition. Read a translation of one song as you hear it.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Shostakovich’s Fifth
immersePlan.text: Play the Fifth Symphony, premiered in Leningrad after a year of danger for the composer. Listen to the slow third movement with your eyes closed.

immersePlan.name: Look at Malevich’s Black Square
immersePlan.text: Look at the black square on white that opened a new direction in painting. Ask what it is, and what it is not. Stay for three minutes and see what you start to notice.

immersePlan.name: Look at El Lissitzky’s Red Wedge
immersePlan.text: Look at the Civil War poster of pure shapes: a red wedge driving into a white circle. It is a landmark of graphic design. Try to draw an idea of your own with just three shapes.

immersePlan.name: Look at the Moscow Metro stations
immersePlan.text: Look at photographs of Moscow Metro stations built as underground palaces, such as Mayakovskaya. Pick the one you would most like to wait in, and say why.

immersePlan.name: Make borscht
immersePlan.text: Cook beetroot soup with potato, cabbage and onion, and serve with a spoon of sour cream. It is a staple from Ukraine across the whole Soviet table. Eat it with black bread.

immersePlan.name: Make or boil pelmeni
immersePlan.text: Make small dumplings by hand, or boil a packet, and eat with butter or vinegar. Families made them in bulk and froze them for winter. Make a batch together if you can.

immersePlan.name: Make blini
immersePlan.text: Make thin pancakes and eat them with jam, sour cream or smoked fish. They are the food of Maslenitsa week before Lent. Roll them up and eat them with your hands.

immersePlan.name: Make strong tea with jam
immersePlan.text: Brew strong tea and drink it with a spoon of jam on the side. Tea makes a long conversation possible. Sit down and let the pot last for an hour.

immersePlan.name: Try kvas
immersePlan.text: Try kvas, a lightly sour, low-alcohol drink made from fermented bread, a summer street drink of the era. If you cannot find it, drink cold sparkling water with a slice of rye toast.

immersePlan.name: Drink a glass of kefir
immersePlan.text: Drink kefir, the cultured milk, a sour drink for breakfast, common across Russia and the Caucasus. Pour a glass, drink it slowly, and notice the tang.

immersePlan.name: Sit before you go
immersePlan.text: Before leaving the house, sit for a minute so nothing is forgotten and the head is calm. It is an old Russian custom, and a pleasant one.

immersePlan.name: Bring an odd number of flowers
immersePlan.text: If you visit someone, bring something small: flowers in an odd number, which are for the living, since even numbers are for funerals. Present them with a smile.

immersePlan.name: Go quiet hunting
immersePlan.text: Go and look for mushrooms or berries or anything patiently found in the woods. Only pick what you can identify with certainty, or simply look. It is tikhaya okhota, a slow pleasure.

immersePlan.name: Play a game of Soviet-school chess
immersePlan.text: Play a game of chess, the way it was taught in Soviet schools, factories and Pioneer palaces. Think before you move, and shake hands afterwards.

immersePlan.name: Play Tetris
immersePlan.text: Play a few rounds of the game written by Alexey Pajitnov on a Soviet Academy of Sciences computer in 1984. Notice how it makes you plan ahead. Stop when you want to stop.

immersePlan.name: Play Durak
immersePlan.text: Play the card game of the fool, where there is no winner, only a last player left holding cards. Play with friends, and laugh at the one who loses.

immersePlan.name: Mark Cosmonautics Day
immersePlan.text: On 12 April the anniversary of Gagarin’s flight is kept. Read a page about Gagarin, look at a photo of him in his orange suit, and say poyekhali out loud.

immersePlan.name: Keep a small Soviet New Year
immersePlan.text: With Christmas discouraged, New Year became the great family holiday. Make an Olivier salad, decorate a small tree, and watch a classic film such as The Irony of Fate with someone.

immersePlan.name: Look up the Tsiolkovsky museum
immersePlan.text: Look up the museum in Kaluga, opened in 1967 in the town where the schoolteacher Tsiolkovsky worked out rocket flight. Read about his idea that humanity cannot live forever in the cradle.

immersePlan.name: Think about dusha
immersePlan.text: Dusha is soul, inner life, warmth. Russians say a person has dusha if they are open, generous and deep. Think of one person you know who has it, and tell them what you see in them.

immersePlan.name: Take chai seriously
immersePlan.text: Chai is tea, and an invitation. Invite someone to chai today, which means a conversation, not just a drink. Put the kettle on first, then ask.

immersePlan.name: Say avos’ about one risk
immersePlan.text: Avos’ means perhaps, hoping it works out, a fatalist shrug. Take one small risk today that you have put off, with avos’. Then notice what happened.

rules.text: Put the shared thing before the private thing once a day
rules.why: The Soviet ideal was collective. Leave the politics aside and keep the habit: one act each day for people other than yourself.

rules.text: Keep the phone out of the room for the long talk
rules.why: The kitchen talk worked because nothing interrupted it. Give a conversation your whole attention, and the kettle can do the rest.

rules.text: Read what is difficult before what is easy
rules.why: Hard books were rationed, copied and treasured. Honour the effort that readers once made for them.
A century of official language made plain speech precious. Practise saying one thing without euphemism.

rules.text: Keep a record: write in a notebook before the day ends
rules.why: Diaries, letters and secret notebooks are why we know what ordinary life felt like.
Hold the culture and the cost together. Do not admire the poems and forget the camps, or the reverse.

read.title: The Master and Margarita
read.creator: Mikhail Bulgakov
read.why: A devil visits Moscow in the 1930s. A satire, a love story and a retelling of Pilate’s story in one.

read.title: One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich
read.creator: Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn
read.why: A single day in a labour camp. Its publication in the Thaw was a national event.

read.title: Life and Fate
read.creator: Vasily Grossman
read.why: A vast novel of Stalingrad and the Soviet century. The KGB seized the manuscript in 1961.

read.title: Requiem
read.creator: Anna Akhmatova
read.why: A cycle of poems about waiting outside a prison for news of her son. Memorised by friends because it could not be written down.

read.title: We
read.creator: Yevgeny Zamyatin
read.why: The first great dystopian novel, written in Soviet Russia. Orwell read it.

read.title: Roadside Picnic
read.creator: Arkady and Boris Strugatsky
read.why: Science fiction about a zone left by visitors. The source for Tarkovsky’s Stalker.

read.title: Secondhand Time
read.creator: Svetlana Alexievich
read.why: Voices of ordinary people after the collapse, collected over decades.

read.title: Everything Was Forever, Until It Was No More
read.creator: Alexei Yurchak
read.why: An anthropologist explains how late Soviet life worked and why its end surprised almost everyone.

read.title: Gulag: A History
read.creator: Anne Applebaum
read.why: The standard history of the camp system. Hard reading that the subject deserves.

watch.title: Battleship Potemkin
watch.creator: Sergei Eisenstein
watch.why: The masterwork of montage, with the Odessa steps sequence.

watch.title: The Cranes Are Flying
watch.creator: Mikhail Kalatozov
watch.why: A wartime love story, and the only Soviet film to win the Palme d’Or at Cannes, in 1958.

watch.title: Solaris
watch.creator: Andrei Tarkovsky
watch.why: A psychologist is sent to a station orbiting an ocean planet. Slow, questioning, unforgettable.

watch.title: Moscow Does Not Believe in Tears
watch.creator: Vladimir Menshov
watch.why: Three women in Moscow across twenty years. It won the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film.

watch.title: Man with a Movie Camera
watch.creator: Dziga Vertov
watch.why: A day of city life without actors or titles, and a landmark of editing.

watch.title: Come and See
watch.creator: Elem Klimov
watch.why: A boy in Belarus in 1943. One of the most harrowing war films ever made. Watch only when ready.

listen.title: Symphony No. 5
listen.creator: Dmitri Shostakovich
listen.why: Premiered in Leningrad after a year of danger for the composer. Its meaning is still argued.

listen.title: String Quartet No. 8
listen.creator: Dmitri Shostakovich
listen.why: Written in three days and dedicated to the victims of war and fascism. A deeply personal piece.

listen.title: Peter and the Wolf
listen.creator: Sergei Prokofiev
listen.why: Written for children’s theatre in Moscow. Each character is an instrument.

listen.title: Songs of Bulat Okudzhava
listen.creator: Bulat Okudzhava
listen.why: A poet with a guitar and a quiet voice who shaped the bard tradition.

listen.title: Gruppa krovi
listen.creator: Kino, led by Viktor Tsoi
listen.why: The best-known album of Leningrad rock at the very end of the Soviet era.

listen.title: Time, Forward
listen.creator: Georgy Sviridov
listen.why: The driving theme later used for the evening television news. Instantly recognisable to anyone who grew up there.

art.title: Black Square
art.creator: Kazimir Malevich
art.why: A black square on white that opened a new direction in painting. Held in the Tretyakov Gallery.

art.title: Beat the Whites with the Red Wedge
art.creator: El Lissitzky
art.why: A poster of pure shapes from the Civil War, and a landmark of graphic design.

art.title: Worker and Kolkhoz Woman
art.creator: Vera Mukhina
art.why: A huge stainless steel sculpture first shown at the Paris World’s Fair, now at VDNKh in Moscow.

art.title: The Moscow Metro stations
art.creator: Various architects
art.why: Stations built as underground palaces. Mayakovskaya, opened in 1938, is a favourite.

art.title: Books
art.creator: Aleksandr Rodchenko
art.why: A poster advertising publishers, with a shouting woman and a famous slogan. A pioneer of photomontage.

eat.title: Borscht
eat.creator: Beetroot soup, with sour cream
eat.why: A staple from Ukraine across the whole Soviet table. Many families have a different recipe.

eat.title: Pelmeni
eat.creator: Small dumplings, with butter or vinegar
eat.why: Made in bulk by families and frozen for winter.

eat.title: Blini
eat.creator: Thin pancakes
eat.why: Eaten with jam, sour cream or caviar. The food of Maslenitsa week before Lent.

eat.title: Kasha
eat.creator: Buckwheat porridge
eat.why: A plain staple that fed millions. Cooked with butter and eaten for breakfast or supper.

eat.title: Olivier salad
eat.creator: Potato, egg, pickle, peas
eat.why: The salad of New Year’s Eve across the Soviet Union.

eat.title: Black rye bread with salt
eat.creator: A slice, plain
eat.why: The most ordinary food in the culture and the most prized.

drink.title: Tea from a samovar or a pot
drink.creator: Strong, with jam
drink.why: The drink that makes a long conversation possible.

drink.title: Kvas
drink.creator: A fermented bread drink
drink.why: Lightly sour and low in alcohol. A summer street drink of the era.

drink.title: Kefir
drink.creator: Cultured milk
drink.why: A sour drink for breakfast, common across Russia and the Caucasus.

customs.title: Sit before a journey
customs.creator: A moment of quiet before leaving
customs.why: An old Russian custom: sit for a minute before setting out so nothing is forgotten and the road goes well.

customs.title: Take your shoes off at the door
customs.creator: Slippers for guests
customs.why: Households keep tapochki, house slippers, ready for visitors.

customs.title: Bring something small when invited
customs.creator: Flowers, in an odd number
customs.why: An odd number of flowers is for the living. Even numbers are for funerals.

customs.title: Quiet hunting
customs.creator: Go and pick mushrooms
customs.why: The Russian phrase "tikhaya okhota" for a patient search in the forest.

customs.title: Visit the banya
customs.creator: A hot steam bath with friends
customs.why: A weekly ritual of heat, birch twigs and tea, shared with friends.

games.title: Chess
games.creator: Board game
games.why: The state taught chess in schools, factories and Pioneer palaces, and Soviet players held the world title almost without a break from 1948 to 1991. Play through one of Mikhail Tal’s games.

games.title: Tetris
games.creator: Video game · Alexey Pajitnov
games.why: Written on an Elektronika 60 at the Soviet Academy of Sciences in Moscow. Seven falling shapes that went round the world.

games.title: Durak
games.creator: Card game · Russia
games.why: The fool: there is no winner, only a last player left holding cards. The most played card game of the Soviet kitchen and the train compartment.

games.title: Papers, Please
games.creator: Video game · Lucas Pope
games.why: You are a border inspector in an invented Eastern Bloc state in 1982. A small, sharp game about rules, shortage and conscience.

festivals.title: New Year
festivals.creator: 31 December
festivals.why: With Christmas discouraged, New Year became the great family holiday from 1935: a decorated fir tree, Grandfather Frost, a table of salads and a toast at midnight.

festivals.title: Cosmonautics Day
festivals.creator: 12 April
festivals.why: The anniversary of Yuri Gagarin’s flight in 1961.

festivals.title: International Women’s Day
festivals.creator: 8 March
festivals.why: A public holiday from 1965, kept with flowers and a day off.

festivals.title: Victory Day
festivals.creator: 9 May
festivals.why: The end of the war in Europe in 1945, which cost the Soviet peoples about 27 million lives. Remembered differently across the former republics today.

festivals.title: Day of Remembrance of the Victims of Political Repression
festivals.creator: 30 October
festivals.why: Names of the executed and imprisoned are read aloud. It began with a hunger strike by prisoners in 1974.

places.title: Museum of Occupations and Freedom Fights
places.creator: Vilnius, Lithuania
places.why: The former KGB headquarters, with its prison cells kept as they were.

places.title: The Corner House
places.creator: Riga, Latvia
places.why: The former KGB building in Riga, open for guided visits to the cells and interrogation rooms.

places.title: Grūtas Park
places.creator: Near Druskininkai, Lithuania
places.why: Dozens of removed Soviet statues set out in a forest, with watchtowers and a period café.

places.title: Karlag Museum
places.creator: Dolinka, Kazakhstan
places.why: The administration building of one of the largest Gulag camp systems, now a museum of those held there.

places.title: Tsiolkovsky State Museum of the History of Cosmonautics
places.creator: Kaluga, Russia
places.why: Opened in 1967 in the town where the schoolteacher worked out rocket flight. Check current travel advice for Russia before planning a visit.

places.title: Moscow Metro
places.creator: Moscow, Russia
places.why: Stations built as palaces for the people from 1935: Mayakovskaya, Komsomolskaya, Ploshchad Revolyutsii. Check current travel advice for Russia before planning a visit.

ethics.title: The common task
ethics.text: The philosopher Nikolai Fyodorov argued that the highest duty of living people is a shared task of care for one another and for the dead. Soviet language borrowed the idea of a shared task and applied it to the state.
ethics.practice: Name one task today that you cannot do alone and ask someone to help.

ethics.title: Truth over comfort
ethics.text: Solzhenitsyn, Akhmatova and Grossman each chose to write the truth when it cost them dearly. Their example is a claim about honesty, not politics.
ethics.practice: Say one true thing you would have preferred to leave unsaid, with kindness.

ethics.title: Remember the victims
ethics.text: Millions died in repression, famine and war. A culture that remembers its poems and forgets its dead has forgotten something essential.
ethics.practice: Read one name or one account from the camps or the terror, and sit with it for a minute.

ethics.title: Mutual help
ethics.text: Under shortage, people relied on favours, shared goods and informal networks. Blat could be unfair, but the habit of help was real and often kind.
ethics.practice: Do one favour today for which you ask nothing in return.

ethics.title: Dignity in small things
ethics.text: In crowded flats and long queues people kept manners, clean clothes and a set table. Dignity was made out of ordinary materials.
ethics.practice: Set the table properly for one meal, even alone.

ethics.title: Private and public
ethics.text: Many people kept two faces: one for the workplace and one for the kitchen. The cost was exhaustion. The gift was an inner life that no one could reach.
ethics.practice: Notice where you perform and where you are plain. Make one small step toward plainness.

philosophy.title: Dialectical materialism
philosophy.text: Marx and Engels held that the world is matter in motion and that change comes through contradiction. The Soviet state made this an official doctrine and taught it in every school. Beyond politics it offers a habit: look for the tension inside a situation and ask how it might resolve.
philosophy.practice: Name a tension in your life and write down both sides before choosing.

philosophy.title: The new person
philosophy.text: The state set out to create a new kind of human being: collective, educated, selfless. Many people sincerely tried, and many were crushed by the demand. It is worth asking what we expect from people and what it costs them.
philosophy.practice: Write down one expectation you place on yourself that you did not choose.

philosophy.title: Cosmism
philosophy.text: Nikolai Fyodorov and then Konstantin Tsiolkovsky imagined humanity growing beyond the Earth and, for Fyodorov, even overcoming death. The Soviet space age grew in that soil. It is ambitious, strange and moving.
philosophy.practice: Look at the night sky for five minutes and ask what a long future would ask of us.

philosophy.title: Socialist realism
philosophy.text: In 1934 the First Congress of Soviet Writers made socialist realism the official style: art should show life in its revolutionary development and serve the people. Great artists worked inside and around it. The question remains: does art serve, or does it tell the truth first?
philosophy.practice: Look at a work of art and ask what it is for.

philosophy.title: Samizdat and conscience
philosophy.text: People typed and passed on banned books at personal risk. They did it because a book that is true does not stay quiet. It is a reminder that reading is an act with consequences.
philosophy.practice: Copy by hand one page that you would not want to lose.

philosophy.title: Social learning
philosophy.text: The psychologist Lev Vygotsky argued that thinking is first shared between people and only later happens inside the head. Children learn by working at the edge of what they can do, with help. The idea has shaped teaching worldwide.
philosophy.practice: Teach something to someone today, or ask someone to teach you.

philosophy.title: Everyday absurdity
philosophy.text: Yurchak describes a late Soviet habit of repeating official words while living by other rules. People were neither believers nor dissidents, but inventors of private meaning. Many of us do the same with our own institutions.
philosophy.practice: Notice one phrase you repeat without meaning it, and consider replacing it.

philosophy.title: Hope against hope
philosophy.text: Nadezhda Mandelstam memorised her husband’s banned poems for decades so that they would not be lost. Her title is a way of saying that meaning survives when people decide to carry it.
philosophy.practice: Learn four lines of a poem by heart.

philosophy.title: Scientific faith
philosophy.text: The Soviet state was devoted to science and technology and also bent them to ideology. Great science happened and so did great harm. Both belong in the picture.
philosophy.practice: Ask of one thing you believe: what would change my mind?

philosophy.title: Memory as duty
philosophy.text: After 1991, civil society groups collected the names and stories of the repressed so that the facts could not be erased. Memory is a form of work, not only a feeling.
philosophy.practice: Write down one story from your family’s past before it is lost.

dayThemes: The last days of a country

intro: The Soviet Union was a one-party state that existed from 1922 to 1991 and covered one sixth of the Earth’s land. It grew out of the Russian Revolution of 1917 and set out to build a society without private ownership of the means of production, guided by the ideas of Karl Marx and Vladimir Lenin. It reached the first artificial satellite and the first person in space. It also ran a vast system of forced labour camps, caused famine through collectivisation, and executed or imprisoned millions of its own people.

This Onda does not ask you to admire or condemn a regime. It asks you to enter the daily world of people who lived inside it. They were many nations, not one: Russians, Ukrainians, Georgians, Armenians, Kazakhs, Estonians, Jews, Tatars and dozens more, whose experiences differed sharply. Many of them cared for children, read poems, argued over tea, grew potatoes at a dacha and tried to be decent in difficult circumstances.

Three threads run through the fortnight. The first is the shared task: the idea, noble in origin and abused in practice, that people owe one another work and care. The second is the kitchen table: the late Soviet habit of talking at length with a few trusted people, away from official language. The third is the long reading: the discipline of reading hard books, sometimes in secret, sometimes copied by hand.

The culture produced work of world importance. Shostakovich wrote symphonies and quartets under political pressure. Eisenstein and Tarkovsky changed what film could be. Akhmatova memorised her own poems because writing them was dangerous. Bulgakov wrote a novel for the drawer that was published decades after his death. Scientists and engineers, many of them imprisoned at some point, built the rockets that opened space.

It is also a story of fear. In 1937 and 1938 alone roughly 680,000 people were shot in the Great Terror. An estimated eighteen million passed through the camps and colonies of the Gulag between 1930 and 1953. Famine in 1932 and 1933 killed millions in Ukraine, Kazakhstan and the Volga region. About 26 to 27 million Soviet citizens died in the Second World War. Any honest way into this culture holds those numbers in view.

The practices here are small on purpose: a morning routine, a long talk, a shared chore, a book. They do not reconstruct Soviet life. They borrow some of its habits at their best and ask you, each day, to remember what those habits cost.
guide.origin: The Soviet Union, from Russia across Ukraine, Belarus, the Caucasus, Central Asia and the Baltic states

figures.name: Konstantin Tsiolkovsky
figures.bio: A schoolteacher in Kaluga, partly deaf from childhood, who worked out the mathematics of rocket flight in 1903 and imagined human life beyond Earth.

figures.name: Anna Akhmatova
figures.bio: Poet of St Petersburg whose husband was shot and son imprisoned. Her cycle Requiem names the grief of a nation.

figures.name: Mikhail Bulgakov
figures.bio: Doctor turned playwright and novelist. The Master and Margarita was published in a censored form in 1966 and 1967.

figures.name: Dmitri Shostakovich
figures.bio: Composer of fifteen symphonies and fifteen string quartets, who lived under constant pressure from the state.

figures.name: Sergei Eisenstein
figures.bio: Pioneer of film editing. Battleship Potemkin, 1925, taught filmmakers around the world.

figures.name: Andrei Tarkovsky
figures.bio: Director of Ivan’s Childhood, Solaris, Stalker and Mirror. He left the Soviet Union in 1982 and did not return.

figures.name: Sergei Korolev
figures.bio: Chief designer of the Soviet space programme. He survived the Gulag and his name was kept secret until after his death.

figures.name: Yuri Gagarin
figures.bio: First person in space, on 12 April 1961, in a flight of 108 minutes. He died in a training jet crash.

figures.name: Andrei Sakharov
figures.bio: Physicist who helped build the Soviet hydrogen bomb and later became a leading human rights campaigner. Nobel Peace Prize, 1975.

figures.name: Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn
figures.bio: Writer who survived the camps and described them. Nobel Prize in Literature, 1970. Expelled from the USSR in 1974.

figures.name: Vasily Grossman
figures.bio: War correspondent at Stalingrad and author of Life and Fate. The manuscript was seized by the KGB and published abroad only in 1980.

figures.name: Nadezhda Mandelstam
figures.bio: Widow of the poet Osip Mandelstam, who memorised his poems and wrote two memoirs of the Stalin years.

figures.name: Lev Vygotsky
figures.bio: Psychologist who argued that thought grows through social interaction. He died of tuberculosis at 37.

history.detail: In February the tsar abdicated and a provisional government took over. In October the Bolsheviks, led by Lenin, seized power in Petrograd and began to build a one-party state.
Red and White armies, foreign interventions and local uprisings devastated the country. Millions died from fighting, hunger and disease, and the Bolsheviks won.
Russia, Ukraine, Belarus and the Transcaucasian republics signed a treaty creating the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics. More republics joined later.
The state set targets for heavy industry and forced farmers into collective farms. Output rose in some sectors, while resistance and hunger followed in the countryside.
Collectivisation and grain requisitions produced a famine that killed millions in Ukraine, Kazakhstan and the Volga region. In Ukraine it is known as the Holodomor.
Mass arrests and executions swept through the party, the army and ordinary society. Archives record roughly 680,000 people shot in these two years.
After Germany invaded in June 1941 the Soviet Union fought the largest land war in history. An estimated 26 to 27 million Soviet citizens died.

history.what: Stalin dies, and the Secret Speech
history.detail: Stalin died in March 1953. In February 1956 Khrushchev denounced his crimes in a closed speech to the Twentieth Party Congress, opening the period called the Thaw.
Sputnik reached orbit on 4 October 1957. Yuri Gagarin flew on 12 April 1961, and Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman in space in June 1963.
Solzhenitsyn’s story of one camp day appeared in the magazine Novy Mir in November 1962 with Khrushchev’s consent, an extraordinary moment of openness.
A long period of stability and slow decline, later called stagnation. Dissidents were tried and exiled, and the kitchen became the place for frank talk.
Mikhail Gorbachev introduced perestroika and glasnost. The Chernobyl disaster of April 1986 exposed the system’s secrecy. The Soviet Union was dissolved on 26 December 1991.

concepts.text: The group that shares a task.
concepts.detail: Workplaces, classes and apartment buildings were organised as collectives that set goals, shared praise and applied pressure. It could be warm or stifling. The ideal asked people to put the group first, and the reality often asked them to conform.

concepts.text: Reality is matter in motion; change comes through contradiction.
concepts.detail: The official philosophy of the state, drawn from Marx and Engels. It taught that history moves through struggles between opposing forces. In practice it became a doctrine to be recited, but its core question, where is the contradiction here, is still useful.

concepts.text: The ideal citizen the state hoped to create.
concepts.detail: Collective, educated, hardworking, free of selfishness. Posters, schools, youth organisations and films promoted the image. Many people tried sincerely to meet it, and the gap between the ideal and ordinary people was a source of pain and humour.

concepts.text: A philosophy of humanity’s future in space.
concepts.detail: Nikolai Fyodorov proposed in the nineteenth century that humanity’s duty is to overcome death and care for the whole cosmos. Tsiolkovsky carried the thought into rocketry. It runs from a strange nineteenth-century library clerk to the first spaceflight.

People typed manuscripts with carbon paper and passed them on, often with a deadline of one night per reader. Poetry, novels, protests and news circulated this way. It created a community of readers bound by risk.

concepts.text: The official style of art from 1934.
concepts.detail: Declared at the First Congress of Soviet Writers, it demanded that art show life in its revolutionary development and serve the people. Some works are formulaic. Others are great, made by artists who worked within its limits.

concepts.text: Frank conversation among friends at home.
concepts.detail: In the 1960s to 1980s, flats were small and shared, and the kitchen was where tea, argument and trust happened. People who were cautious in public said what they thought there. It shaped a generation of thinkers and writers.

concepts.text: Favours and connections that get things done.
concepts.detail: In an economy of shortages, a friend in a shop or a ministry was worth more than a salary. Blat was both unfair and a web of mutual help. Understanding it explains much of daily life.

concepts.text: The cultural opening after Stalin’s death.
concepts.detail: From the mid 1950s to the mid 1960s writers, filmmakers and poets pressed against limits. Solzhenitsyn was published, poetry readings filled stadiums, and young people felt that reform from within was possible. The opening closed again, but its memory lasted.

Lev Vygotsky argued that children learn first in conversation and cooperation, and only later internalise what they have learned. His "zone of proximal development" describes what a person can do with help but not yet alone, and it still shapes teaching.

facts.text: The first communist subbotniks were held in spring 1919 by railway workers on the Moscow to Kazan line. Lenin praised them that summer in a pamphlet called A Great Beginning.
Sergei Korolev, who led the Soviet space programme, spent years in prison and the Kolyma camps before being brought back to work on rockets. His name was a state secret until he died.
Late Soviet allotments were limited to about six hundred square metres, known as "six sotok". On such plots families grew a large share of the country’s potatoes, vegetables and fruit.
The Moscow Metro opened on 15 May 1935. Stations built in the following years, such as Mayakovskaya in 1938, were decorated with marble, mosaics and chandeliers as public palaces.
Chess was taught in schools and treated as a point of national pride. Mikhail Botvinnik became the first Soviet world champion in 1948.
The Master and Margarita was first published in a censored version in the magazine Moskva in 1966 and 1967. Readers retyped the cut passages and passed them around.
The Cranes Are Flying won the Palme d’Or at Cannes in 1958, and is still the only Soviet film to have done so.

sensitivity.note: The Soviet Union was a one-party state responsible for mass repression, famine and war crimes, and also home to great art, science and ordinary kindness. This Onda explores the culture, ideas and daily habits of its people. It does not endorse the regime or its successors.
requiredCaveats: Hold the culture and the cost together. The terror, the Gulag and the famines are part of the story and are not set aside.
The Soviet Union was many nations. Ukrainians, Balts, Georgians, Kazakhs and others experienced it as rule from Moscow, often as imperial, and their accounts deserve equal weight with Russian ones.
Russian culture is not the same as any state. Reading Akhmatova or watching Tarkovsky does not endorse any government, past or present.
This content has not yet been reviewed by historians or by people from the former Soviet republics. It should be before release.
